extracted.intended_audience: model aeroplane builders, hobbyists, and early aeronautical experimenters
extracted.subtask_description: Practical and theoretical guidance for designing, building, testing, and competing with model aeroplanes (rubber- and power-driven), emphasizing aerodynamics, weight, stability, motive power and construction materials. A how-to/textbook treatment aimed at hobbyists and experimenters.

rubrics_metrics.name: First requisite: the model shall FLY
rubrics_metrics.description: The first requirement of a model aeroplane, or flying machine, is that it shall FLY.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unless the machine flies it has failed; for ordinary flights and scientific study the model need not be an exact scale replica but should 'approximate to the real thing' along main lines. Record-seeking models may have different priorities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simplicity
rubrics_metrics.description: Simplicity should be the first thing aimed at—simplicity means efficiency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer simple designs over complex ones; simplicity is especially important in models (even more than full-sized machines) to achieve reliable performance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weight: maximum strength with minimum weight
rubrics_metrics.description: How to obtain the maximum strength with the minimum of weight is one of the most difficult problems the student has to solve.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Achieve via (1) knowledge of materials, (2) efficient combination of materials, (3) constant use of a balance and recording weights and trial results. WEIGH EVERYTHING. Heavy models can be better against wind but must fly fast and be well powered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resistance minimization (function of an aeroplane)
rubrics_metrics.description: The function of an aeroplane is to pass through the medium with the minimum disturbance and resistance; every part should be constructed to move through the air with minimum disturbance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Resistance comprises aerodynamic resistance, head resistance and skin-friction. Reduce by smoothing surfaces, using ichthyoid/fish-like contours, minimizing exposed framework, and avoiding unnecessary appendages (e.g., heavy skids).

rubrics_metrics.name: Shape of least head resistance
rubrics_metrics.description: For minimum (head) resistance a body should have: (1) greatest diameter two-fifths of its length from its head; (2) breadth:depth proportion 4:3; (3) length at least 5–9 times greatest breadth (nine better than five); (4) a very tapering stern; (5) all surfaces as smooth as possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A body of such shape gives at most only one-twentieth the resistance of a flat disk of similar area. Apply when designing fuselage/short bodies and propeller housings; modify slightly for twin propellers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Skin-friction awareness and coefficients
rubrics_metrics.description: Skin-friction (surface resistance) is small at low velocities but increases roughly as the square of velocity; Lanchester's and Zahm's experimental coefficients are cited.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use smooth surfaces to reduce skin friction; uneven/rough surfaces increase coefficients markedly. Use given formula and tabulated values to estimate friction for given length and speed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Material of aerofoil affects resistance (fabric vs wood/metal)
rubrics_metrics.description: Fabric-covered planes offer considerably more resistance than wooden or metal ones; built-up fabric gains in lightness but loses in resistance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose aerofoil material balancing lightness and skin resistance—polished wood or metal surfaces give lower resistance and are better for higher speeds and heavier models.

rubrics_metrics.name: Automatic stability essential
rubrics_metrics.description: Any model flying machine (in the absence of a pilot) must possess a high degree of automatic stability; it must be naturally stable in the medium through which it is proposed to drive it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider both theoretical and practical aspects; designs must ensure oscillations are damped, and stability characteristics can change with speed and flight regime.

rubrics_metrics.name: Centres coincidence and propeller line
rubrics_metrics.description: For stability: the centres of gravity, of pressure, of head resistance, should be coincident, and the propulsive action of the propeller pass through this same point.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If centres do not coincide the arrangement becomes acentric and produces upsetting couples—common cause of failures. In practice some put CG slightly above centre of head resistance to counter gust-lift, but deviations must be small and deliberate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Propeller shaft should pass through centre of gravity
rubrics_metrics.description: The propeller shaft should pass through the centre of gravity of the machine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This avoids acentric propulsive action that tends to upset the machine and complicates stability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Longitudinal stability: front planes angle greater than rear
rubrics_metrics.description: The front planes should be at a greater angle of inclination than the rear ones.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This arrangement aids longitudinal stability; also note longitudinal stability decreases as the aeroplane rises (monoplane can become unstable when angle of ascent exceeds main aerofoil inclination).

rubrics_metrics.name: Dihedral and transverse stability rules
rubrics_metrics.description: The dihedral angle affects transverse stability; excessive dihedral or a very low centre of gravity can cause dangerous pitching motions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose dihedral to balance transverse stability with undesirable pitching tendencies; different forms of dihedral (upturned tips, etc.) have distinct effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three planes more stable than two
rubrics_metrics.description: Three planes are more stable than two [elevator—main aerofoil—horizontal rudder behind].
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use additional surfaces (e.g., tail/elevator) to increase natural stability, especially in gliders or unmanned models.

rubrics_metrics.name: Large moment of inertia is inimical to stability
rubrics_metrics.description: A large moment of inertia is opposed to stability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid concentrating mass far from the CG; design to minimize inertial moments that resist damping of oscillations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stability can change with speed
rubrics_metrics.description: Aeroplanes naturally stable up to a certain velocity may become unstable when moving beyond that speed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Account for aerodynamic changes (turbulence, flow separation, deformation) at higher speeds when designing and testing; stability must be validated across expected speed range.

rubrics_metrics.name: Camber, angle of incidence, and centre of pressure effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Camber and angle of incidence determine centre of pressure; arched surfaces exhibit centre of pressure movement and reversal; deep camber can cause instability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select camber and angle of incidence to place centre of pressure appropriately relative to CG; prefer most efficient camber (author discusses) and be cautious of excessively cambered surfaces which are unstable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aspect ratio importance
rubrics_metrics.description: Aspect ratio (span divided by chord) affects sustentation and centre of pressure behavior.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Higher aspect ratios (longer span relative to chord) generally improve performance but influence structural and resistance trade-offs; consult provided tables and experiments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Propeller design and selection criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Key propeller factors: position of propeller, number of blades, fan vs propeller, pitch, slip, thrust, pitch coefficient (ratio), diameter, theoretical pitch, uniform pitch, blade area, rate of rotation, shrouding, blade shape and contour; methods to ascertain pitch and to experimentally measure static thrust.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design propellers by considering desired thrust and rpm, use experiments (author's and Havilland's setups) to measure dynamic thrust, prefer hollow-faced or built-up blades as appropriate, and consider twin-propeller arrangements for torque balance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rubber (twisted) motors: behaviour and optimisation
rubrics_metrics.description: Rubber motors: experiments on extension, laws of elongation and permanent set, torque vs strand number and length, analogy with springs, number of revolutions and maximum turns, lubricants, action of copper and water, preservation, testing, shape and size of section, geared rubber motors and their practical difficulties/advantages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design rubber motors by testing specific rubber strands, recording torque and revolutions, preserve rubber from deleterious effects (water, copper), use lubrication carefully, and prefer a long motor for efficiency—gearing may be used but has practical trade-offs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Other motive power considerations (spring, compressed air, steam, petrol, electric)
rubrics_metrics.description: Spring motors are inferior to rubber; compressed air motors are promising on paper but have practical drawbacks; steam engines present boiler/difficulty issues (Langley experiments); petrol motors limited by size; electric motors also discussed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select motive power by weighing complexity, weight, achievable power-to-weight, and practical construction difficulties; small steam/petrol/electric models face severe size/weight constraints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Materials selection limited and critical
rubrics_metrics.description: Choice of materials is strictly limited: bamboo, ash, spruce, whitewood, poplar, steel (including umbrella-section), steel wire, silk, aluminium, magnalium, alloys, ebonite, vulcanized fibre, celluloid, mica, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose material for appropriate strength-to-weight and surface finish; author emphasizes knowledge of materials and how to combine them to get maximum strength for minimum weight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construction practices and 'things to avoid'
rubrics_metrics.description: Hints: principle of continuity in general design, importance of soldering, things to avoid, aerofoil of metal/wood/fabric, how to camber without ribs, flexible joints, single surfaces, rod or tube for rubber motor, position of rubber, position of centre of pressure, elevators and tails, skids vs wheels, shock absorbers, relation between gap and chord.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow sound construction techniques, avoid unnecessary appendages and heavy chassis, use appropriate fastening/soldering, place rubber motor and control surfaces to achieve desired CG and stability; practical building tips provided throughout chapter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Steering and torque management
rubrics_metrics.description: Steering difficulties: effects of propeller torque and methods to obviate it (two-propeller solution is only partial success), speed solution, vertical fins, balancing tips/ailerons, weighting, canting the elevator transversely, and the necessity for some form of keel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design steering to counteract propeller torque (consider twin screws, differential arrangements, fin/aileron use), and include some keel/fin surfaces for yaw stability and directional control.

rubrics_metrics.name: Launching technique and parameters
rubrics_metrics.description: Launching considerations: direction to launch, launch velocity, wooden vs fabric aerofoils behavior, launching apparatus (Poynter's), launching very light models, large/power-driven model launch methods, setting of elevator, suitable propellers, Kress' method, twin-screw launching, pre-rotating propellers, and best angle to launch.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adjust launch angle and pre-rotation to model design; light fabric models and heavy wooden models behave differently—select appropriate launching technique and propeller for takeoff behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scale model limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Scale models of actual flying machines that will fly mean models at least 10 or 12 feet across; smaller scale reproductions cannot include working motors or framework at scale weight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that full-scale fidelity is constrained by powerplant, component scaling, and weight—very small scale 'true' models are impractical for flight; plan scale targets accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimental method, record keeping and empirical formulae
rubrics_metrics.description: From experiments empirical formulas can be obtained which combined with mathematical induction/deduction lead to generalized laws; keep careful experimental records.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weigh everything, record every trial and modification in writing, use provided formulae and tables (lift/drift, skin friction, propeller thrust, power-speed relations) to compare and rate designs and motors; run controlled experiments to derive efficiencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Competition awareness and classification
rubrics_metrics.description: Model flying competitions have classifications (Aero Models Association's classification) and various points to keep in mind when competing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design and set up models with competition rules and classifications in mind; consider required measures such as flight duration, distance, and weight classes when optimizing a model.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of provided tables and formulae for design calculations
rubrics_metrics.description: Chapter XIV provides useful tables and formulae: comparative velocities, conversions, areas, measures, tables of skin friction, lift and drift on cambered/plane aerofoils, timber data, formulae connecting weight lifted and velocity, power-speed relations, propeller thrust, methods to determine static thrust, I.H.P. of model steam engines, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply these formulae and tables to estimate expected performance, compare designs, compute horse-power and static thrust, and to evaluate motor efficiency and theoretical flight length prior to construction and testing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preservation and testing of rubber (motor) materials
rubrics_metrics.description: Action of copper, water, lubricants, and storage affect rubber; methods to test rubber and preserve it are discussed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid corrosive contacts (copper), protect rubber from water and deleterious chemicals, test samples for torque and elongation before using in a model, and implement preservation techniques to maintain motor performance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Propeller-propulsive-axis alignment
rubrics_metrics.description: The propulsive action should pass through the point where CG/centre of pressure/head resistance coincide; propeller position and shaft alignment are critical for avoiding upsetting couples.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mount propeller(s) to deliver thrust through the CG region; misalignment leads to acentric forces and destabilizing moments.
